lyle always an interesting pursuit to trace any great result to its primary source. Whether it be the exploration of a great river through swamps and hostile tribes; or • great principle through opposition, Rt.., judice, ill will, and misrepreeentation, it is exhilarating to note difficulties successfully overcome, and to grasp the hand, as it were, of the hero in the strife. Most vict rims in this world are the outcome of hard work and persistent effort; it is only by patient labour that the true origin of great movements can be dieoovered. It is ratioh easier to tell the date tv.d cause of the Corn Law imposition, than to say when the first efforts were made for its repeal. lii such movements there are generally the silent, unostentatious actions of the unknown, long before any public recognition is made. Thus it ' wee with the repeal of the Corn Laws. Mr. , Prentice in his" History of the League." I I claims this position of honour for the I Liberals who fought the battle at the first election for Manchester, after the Reform Act of 1833, "thus Thomson's Committee," ear he, " was the precursor of the Anti. Corn Law League in the great work of pub. lie instruction. Before we turn to Mr. Ash- worth's history of the origin of the League, it will be well, perhaps, to refer to the causal of the imposition of the odious tax, and to I make some mention of the effects upon the I great mass of our fellow-countrymen. A 1 corn tax was an unknown thing in England I till after the close of the great French war in I 1815. In those comparatively early days I the manufactures of the country were not I of paramount importance. They wee] I rapidly taking a foremost position, but so far t e products of the Boil were the chief con- sideration. And naturally so, A prosper. our manufacturing industry cleated a new class of rich men who began to compete I both in wealth and position with the old' feudal aristocracy; hence jealousies arose. I During the war, when our ports were vir- I tually closed the nation had to depend for its, food supplies upon what the soil could pros I duce. In good years this was nearly sta.. theme, but in years of bad harvests the sup- I ply was lamentably deficient both in qualityl and quantity. The restriction had the effects I of raising the price of food to a high standard, farmers reaped large profit., and landlords I gathered in fat rents. With peace all this I was changed. With free imports prices fell I and rents followed suit. Both farmers and landlords thought they saw ruin staring them in the face, and as they were the great I power of the state they soon made matters right by fixing a sliding scale of duties on imports which kept the price of grain at famine prices, and which prohibited the im- port of" flee " whether alive or dead. Among Mr. Ashworth's elaborate statistics none are more interesting than those which prove how much better fed the people of to- day are than were their grandfathers. With this scarcity of food there naturally followed discontent, bad trade, and lawlesa- nee/. This did not follow in an invariable ratio ; but it came in separate periods, and with increasing force and volume. The cause is not far to seek.
